segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: Excuse me, Or Johnson. May I speak to you for a minute?

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Sure. Come in.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: I'm Melanie Griffin. I'm taking your course in Population Studies.

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Right. Well, Melanie, how can I help you?

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: I'm . . . having a bit of trouble with the second assignment, and it's due in twelve days.

segments.speaker: OR JOHNSON
segments.en: What sort of trouble are you having? Is the assignment question a problem?

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: Well, that's part of the problem. I'm also having- been having- trouble getting hold of the books. I've been to the library several times, and all the books are out.

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Sounds like you should have started borrowing books a bit earlier.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: Well, I had a really big assignment due in for another course. and I've been spending all my time on that, and I thought ...

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: ... You might get an extension of time to finish your assignment for me?

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: If that's possible, but I don't know . ..

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Well, yes, it is possible, but extensions are normally given only for medical or compassionate reasons, otherwise it's really a question of organising your study, and we don't like giving extensions to students who simply didn't plan their work properly. What did you get for your first assignment?

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: I got eighty-seven per cent.

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Mmm, yes. you did very well indeed, so obviously you can produce good work.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: I don't think I'll need too much extra time, as long as I can get hold of some of the important references.

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Well. since you did so well in your first assignment. I'm prepared to give you an extra two weeks for this one, so that'll mean you'll need to submit it about a month from now.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: Thank you . . DR JOHN SON: Now, what about the reading materials? Have you checked out the journal articles in the list?

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: Umm, no, not yet, there were about twenty of them, and I wasn't sure which ones would be most useful or important.

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Well, they're all useful, but I don't expect anyone to read them all, because a number of them deal with the same issues. Let me give you some suggestions. The article by Anderson and Hawker is really worth reading.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: Right, I'll read that one.

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: You should also read the article by Jackson, but just look at the part on the research methodology- how they did it.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: OK . .. Jackson, got that ...

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: And if you have time, the one by Roberts says very relevant things, although it's not essential.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: So, OK. if it's~ . I'll try and read that one . . .

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Now, the one by Morris. I wouldn't bother with that at this stage, if I were you.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: OK. I won't bother with Morris. Oh, now, someone told me the article by Cooper is important.

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Well. yes. in a way, but just look at the last part. where he discusses the research results. And lastly. there's Forster- I can't think why I included that one. It's not bad and could be of some help. but not that much.

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Now, let's deal with the assignment question. What's the problem there?

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: It's the graph on page two.

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: What seems to be the problem? It's just the bar graph showing reasons why people change where they live. ·

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: Well, I've got a photocopy but the reasons at the bottom are missing.

segments.speaker: OR JOHNSON
segments.en: Ab, OK. Look at the first bar on the graph- now that indicates the number of people who move because they want more space.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: Oh I see . .. bar one. OK . .. Now what about the next bar?

segments.speaker: OR JOHN SON
segments.en: Bar two is to do with the people living neartzy disturbing them, so they chose to move away to somewhere quieter. Now let's look at bar number three .. . another reason people change their place of living is because they want to be closer to the city.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: OK. Proximity to the city is an issue .. .

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Now . . . bar number four refers to problems when the owner of the property won't help fix things that go wrong. In other words, the owner is not helpful and so the tenants move out.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: OK .. . Now what about bar five?

segments.speaker: OR JOHN SON
segments.en: Bar five is about those people who move because they need a bus or train to get them into the city or to go to work.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: OK .. . And bar six?

segments.speaker: DR JOHNSON
segments.en: Bar number six is interesting. That reason was given quite a lot- people moving because they wanted to be in a more attractive neighbourhood.

segments.speaker: MELANIE
segments.en: Oh, yes, thank you very much.
